verdict.rationale: AWS documents OIDC identity providers that connect external CI such as GitHub Actions to AWS, and role assumption that returns temporary session credentials, since roles carry no long-term access keys. That covers the core short-lived-credential federation path for CI. The 'nothing ships a long-lived key' guarantee and the end-to-end documentation are not shown in the evidence, so this is partial rather than full. missing for 10: an end-to-end setup walkthrough for OIDC trust and role assumption from CI, workload identity for services running on AWS, a mechanism to enforce or block long-lived access keys, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a security engineer, nothing ships a long-lived key — OIDC/workload identity federation issues short-lived credentials to CI and services, documented end to end

citations.quote: OIDC connects applications, like GitHub Actions, that do not run on AWS to AWS resources.
when you assume a role, it provides you with temporary security credentials for your role session.
a role does not have standard long-term credentials such as a password or access keys associated with it.
With an identity provider (IdP), you can manage your user identities outside of AWS and give these external user identities permissions to use AWS resources in your account.
